Source: https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-bot.html

## The policy robot[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-bot.html#the-policy-robot)

This page explains what the policy robot does every Monday, what it opens on the CREED project, how it is set up, and how a person reviews its work.

### What the robot does[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-bot.html#what-the-robot-does)

The policy robot is `bin/policy-bot.php run` (the logic is `src/Bot/PolicyBot.php`). Once a week it runs the full refresher, [`bin/refresh-policy.php`](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-refresh.html), which re-reads the upstream sources for support dates, latest patches and new version lines. Then it turns the refresher's exit code and report into one of four outcomes:

| Refresher exit | What the robot does |
| --- | --- |
| `0` nothing worth committing | Nothing, unless `refreshed_on` is 7 or more days old: then it runs the refresher again with `--touch` (the weekly heartbeat) and treats that run like any other. |
| `3` changes written | Commits `policy/policy.json` and `policy/sources.json` on `auto/policy-refresh` and pushes a merge request set to merge on its own when its pipeline passes. |
| `4` something held or refused | Commits whatever was written (often nothing) the same way, but the merge request waits for a person. |
| `1` hard failure | Stops with exit 1. The job goes red and nothing is pushed. |

After a handled run it also brings its [alert issues](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-bot.html#the-alert-issues) in line with the report.

Note

The robot only ever stages `policy/policy.json` and `policy/sources.json`. It never tags, releases or touches code, and nothing it writes reaches `main` except through a merge request and its pipeline.

What it may write is decided by the refresher's change classes: a date that moves earlier (`tighten`), a new patch or a new line (`neutral`) and a later `active_until` (`loosen-warning`) are written; a later `security_until` (`loosen-fail`) is held until two sources or 14 days of the same answer prove it; removing anything, or touching `tools` or `rules`, is refused. [Refreshing the policy](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-refresh.html) has the full table.

### The merge request[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-bot.html#the-merge-request)

A run that has something to commit opens (or updates) one merge request:

- **Title:** `policy: refresh from upstream sources`, also the commit message. The committer is `CREED policy bot`.
- **Branch:** `auto/policy-refresh` into the default branch, with "delete source branch" set.
- **Label:** `auto-data`.
- **Auto-merge:** only after an exit 3 (everything that changed was written). After an exit 4 a person merges or closes it.
- **Body:** the date of the run, then one line per change in the refresher's own words, `php 8.3: latest_patch 8.3.35 -> 8.3.36 [neutral]`, under `Changes:`, `Held:` and `Refused:`, then any `Disagreements:` between sources and any `Sources that failed this run:`.

The robot force-pushes `auto/policy-refresh` on every run, so the branch always holds the latest refresh and an open merge request is updated rather than duplicated. Anything a person commits to that branch is overwritten on the next Monday.

### The alert issues[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-bot.html#the-alert-issues)

People hear from the robot through GitLab issues, one per alert key, labeled `auto-alert` and titled `[auto-alert] <key>`:

| Key | Opened when |
| --- | --- |
| `held:<component>:<line>:<field>` | the refresher held a change (a later `security_until` not yet proven) |
| `refused:<component>:<line>:<field>` | the refresher refused a change (a removal, or a `tools` or `rules` edit) |
| `disagreement:<component>:<line>:<field>` | two sources disagree and the policy sides with neither |
| `upcoming-eol:<component>:<line>` | a listed line's `security_until` is 60 days away or less |

A key that is still there on a later run gets a note on its open issue instead of a second issue. A key that is gone closes its issue with a "Cleared on" note. The logic is `src/Bot/AlertIssues.php`.

### Reviewing what it opens[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-bot.html#reviewing-what-it-opens)

1. **Read the merge request body first.** Each change line names the component, the line, the field, the old and new value and its class. Check a date against its source: php.net for PHP, the Node.js release schedule for Node, endoflife.date for the rest.
2. **Let a green exit 3 merge itself.** Its changes are all `tighten`, `neutral` or `loosen-warning`, and `composer ci` has passed on them.
3. **Read the pipeline when it is red.** A red pipeline blocks the auto-merge. Whether the failure is in the policy (the schema validator or a test) or unrelated (for example a new security advisory in `composer audit`), fix it on `main`, then bring the branch up to date: the merge request's Rebase button, or start the robot by hand (Build > Pipelines > Run pipeline on `main`), which rebuilds the branch from the new `main`. Re-running the old pipeline alone tests the old branch again. Never push a fix to `auto/policy-refresh`: the next run overwrites it.
4. **Decide the held and refused items by hand.** They are in the merge request body and each has an `auto-alert` issue. A held `security_until` that you can prove from the vendor's page goes in by a normal merge request that cites the source; the issue closes itself on the next run.
5. **After a merge,** the copies downstream are stale until refreshed: see [Carrying CREED in another package](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/carrying-creed.html). A release of CREED is still a person's call ([Contributing](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/contributing.html)).

### How it is scheduled[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-bot.html#how-it-is-scheduled)

The `policy-bot` job in `.gitlab-ci.yml` runs the robot in two cases only: a scheduled pipeline whose schedule carries the variable `CREED_JOB=policy-bot`, and a pipeline started by hand from the web. CREED's schedule runs it on `main` every Monday. The check-only [`refresh-patches`](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/patch-refresh.html) job skips that schedule, so a robot pipeline runs only the robot. `GIT_DEPTH: "0"` gives the job the full history it needs to force-push its branch.

Without the token the job prints "CREED_BOT_TOKEN not set; skipping the policy robot" and stays green.

### Setting it up[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-bot.html#setting-it-up)

The setup lives in GitLab project settings, not in this repo. To set it up on CREED again, or on a fork:

1. **A project access token** (Settings > Access tokens): role Maintainer (Developer works only if Developers may merge to the default branch), scopes `api` (merge requests and alert issues) and `write_repository` (the push), an expiry of 90 days, then rotate.
2. **A CI/CD variable `CREED_BOT_TOKEN`** holding the token: masked and hidden, protected, not a file. The schedule runs on `main`, a protected branch, so the protected variable reaches it.
3. **A pipeline schedule on `main`** (Build > Pipeline schedules): weekly on Monday, with the variable `CREED_JOB` = `policy-bot`.
4. **Leave `auto/policy-refresh` unprotected,** or the robot cannot push it.

The robot also reads GitLab's predefined variables (listed in [Configuration](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/configuration.html)); a real run that is missing any of them stops with exit 1 before it commits or pushes, and names the missing variables (names only, never values).

Warning

Every line the robot prints, including git's own errors and the command echoes, passes through one mask that replaces the token with `[masked]`, and the token travels only in the push URL and the `PRIVATE-TOKEN` header. Still: keep the variable masked, and rotate the token if a job log ever shows it.

### Trying it without GitLab[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-bot.html#trying-it-without-gitlab)

A dry run needs no token and changes nothing. It prints the outcome it would choose, the files it would commit, the merge request title and body, and the alert issues it would open:

```
php bin/policy-bot.php run --dry-run
php bin/policy-bot.php run --dry-run --offline tests/fixtures/feeds
```

`--offline` reads saved feeds instead of fetching them; `tests/fixtures/feeds/` carries a full set. Creed Bratton ran a dry run once, at the quarry. Nobody asked what it printed.

### Related[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-bot.html#related)

- [Refreshing the policy](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-refresh.html)
- [Keeping the patches fresh](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/patch-refresh.html)
- [Commands and exit codes](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/commands.html)
- [Configuration](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/configuration.html)
- [Troubleshooting](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/troubleshooting.html)

## Refreshing the policy[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-refresh.html#refreshing-the-policy)

This page explains how `bin/refresh-policy.php` keeps every support date, patch and new line in `policy/policy.json` tied to a canonical source, so nobody types a date by hand.

### Sources per component[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-refresh.html#sources-per-component)

PHP dates come from php.net, Node dates from the Node.js release schedule, and Laravel, MySQL, Vue and Composer from endoflife.date; patches come from php.net, nodejs.org, Packagist and npm.

### Change classes[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-refresh.html#change-classes)

Each run sorts every change into a class:

| Class | What it is | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tighten` | a date moves earlier, or a `current` line gets its first end date | written |
| `neutral` | a new `latest_patch`, or a new line above every listed line | written |
| `loosen-warning` | `active_until` moves later (a warning tier, never a failure) | written |
| `loosen-fail` | `security_until` moves later, or an EOL line would be supported again | held, unless two independent sources agree (php.net and endoflife.date for PHP, schedule.json and endoflife.date for Node) or `policy/sources.json` shows the same value from the same source for 14 days |
| `refused` | removing a line or a date, or any change to `tools` or `rules` | never automatic; reported (a Composer minimum on an EOL line shows up here) |

### When a source is down[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-refresh.html#when-a-source-is-down)

A source that is down, slow or returns something unreadable changes nothing: its fields keep their last good value. A line missing from a feed is never removed. Where a first-party source and endoflife.date disagree, the first party wins and the disagreement is reported.

### Running the refresher[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-refresh.html#running-the-refresher)

```
php bin/refresh-policy.php [--dry-run] [--offline <dir>] [--policy <path>]
    [--sources <path>] [--report <file>] [--today YYYY-MM-DD] [--touch]
```

`--report` writes JSON with `changes`, `held`, `refused`, `disagreements` and `source_errors`. `--touch` sets `refreshed_on` to today even when nothing else changed (the weekly heartbeat). `policy/sources.json` records, per value, which source said it, and the first and last day it was seen.

### Exit codes[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-refresh.html#exit-codes)

Exit codes: `0` nothing worth committing (always `0` with `--dry-run`); `1` hard failure; `3` something was written to `policy/policy.json` or `policy/sources.json`, including a released `loosen-fail` (the policy robot raises the alert from the report); `4` something was held or refused. The refresher itself never commits: whatever it could write is written either way, and on exit 4 the held or refused items stay out of the file.

What happens next is the [policy robot](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-bot.html)'s job: on exit 3 it opens a merge request that merges itself when its pipeline passes; on exit 4 it opens one that waits for a person, plus an `auto-alert` issue per held or refused item.

`bin/refresh-patches.php` still works as before.

### Related[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-refresh.html#related)

- [Keeping the patches fresh](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/patch-refresh.html)
- [The policy robot](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-bot.html)
- [Policy file format](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/policy-format.html)

Source: https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html

## Quick start[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html#quick-start)

This page takes you from an empty project to two real answers from the CREED reader in four steps.

### Steps[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html#steps)

1. **Require it.** Add CREED to your project.
   ```sh
   composer require waynestate/creed
   ```
2. **Load the bundled policy.** The package ships its policy file, and `Policy::bundled()` loads it.
   ```php
   use Waynestate\Creed\Policy;
   
   $policy = Policy::bundled();
   ```
   Expected result: a loaded policy. `origin()` says where it came from.
3. **Ask `stateOf`.** What state is PHP 8.2 in, on this date?
   ```php
   use Waynestate\Creed\State;
   
   $state = $policy->stateOf('php', '8.2', new DateTimeImmutable('2026-10-27'));
   // State::Security
   ```
   Expected result: `State::Security`. The answer is the state of that version on that date, nothing else.
4. **Ask `oldestSupported`.** What is the oldest PHP an app may declare?
   ```php
   $floor = $policy->oldestSupported('php', new DateTimeImmutable('2026-10-27'));
   // '8.2'
   ```
   Expected result: `'8.2'`, the lowest version still Active or Security.

### What you built[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html#what-you-built)

Two questions, two stamped answers: the state of a version on a date, and the floor an app may declare. One last time: the reader answers, it does not guess.

### Next steps[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html#next-steps)

- Read every public member in the [Reader API](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html).
- See how a version moves between states in [Support states and the grace period](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/support-states.html).
- [Install](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html) covers developing on CREED itself.

### Related[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html#related)

- [Overview](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/index.html)
- [Install](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html)
- [Reader API](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html)
- [Contributing](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/contributing.html)

## Reading the policy from PHP[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/reading-the-policy.html#reading-the-policy-from-php)

This page shows how a PHP program loads the CREED policy and asks it the one question every tool needs: what state is this version in, on this date?

### Load a policy[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/reading-the-policy.html#load-a-policy)

CREED is the Wayne State app stack's version policy, as data. One file, `policy/policy.json`, lists the support dates for PHP, Laravel, Node, MySQL, Vue and Inertia, plus the rules every check runs against. A small framework-free PHP reader, `Waynestate\Creed\Policy`, answers the questions:

- `Policy::bundled()`, `Policy::fromFile($path)`, `Policy::fromArray($data)`: load a policy; `origin()` says where it came from.

### The example[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/reading-the-policy.html#the-example)

One snippet covers the whole round trip:

```php
use Waynestate\Creed\Policy;
use Waynestate\Creed\State;

$policy = Policy::bundled();

// What state is PHP 8.2 in, on this date?
$state = $policy->stateOf('php', '8.2', new DateTimeImmutable('2026-10-27'));
// State::Security

// What is the oldest PHP an app may declare?
$floor = $policy->oldestSupported('php', new DateTimeImmutable('2026-10-27'));
// '8.2'
```

### stateOf[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/reading-the-policy.html#stateof)

`stateOf($component, $version, $on)`: the state, or an exception; `tryStateOf()` is the same answer as `null` when it cannot be answered. In the example, PHP 8.2 on 2026-10-27 is `State::Security`.

### oldestSupported[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/reading-the-policy.html#oldestsupported)

`oldestSupported($component, $on)`: the lowest version still Active or Security; `supported()` lists all of them, oldest first. In the example, the oldest PHP an app may declare on 2026-10-27 is `'8.2'`.

Tip

One last time: the reader answers, it does not guess.

### Related[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/reading-the-policy.html#related)

- [Support states and the grace period](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/support-states.html)
- [Reader API](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html)
- [Install](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html)
- [Quick start](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html)

## Support states and the grace period[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/support-states.html#support-states-and-the-grace-period)

This page explains how a version moves through the states `Active`, `Security`, `Eol` and `EolGraceExpired`, and what the reader does with versions it has never heard of.

### With Arms Wide Open[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/support-states.html#with-arms-wide-open)

The support window stays open until `security_until`. A version is still `Security` on that day, moves to `Eol` the day after, and stays in `Eol` for `eol_grace_days` (90) more days before it is `EolGraceExpired`. The boundary is inclusive, and the reader never guesses.

![Form CR-1 from the front page, filled in four times from policy.json and stamped: PHP 8.2 on 2026-10-29 is Security only, 63 days left; PHP 8.2 on 2027-01-01 is EOL, in grace until 2027-03-31; PHP 8.1 on 2026-10-29 is past grace; Laravel 13 on 2026-10-29 is Supported.](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/readme/form-cr1.svg)

Form CR-1, as the front page fills it in: four real rows of `policy/policy.json`, the same answers `Policy::stateOf` gives, stamped.

### Versions CREED hasn't heard of[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/support-states.html#versions-creed-hasn-t-heard-of)

The reader refuses what it does not know, except the newest thing and the oldest. A version that sorts above every line the policy lists is `Active`, and `isAheadOfPolicy()` says so. A version that parses and sorts below every listed line is `Eol`: it is older than the oldest listed line, and that is end of life by definition. `belowOldestLineReason()` gives the reason, `older than the oldest listed line (8.1)`. A version that falls between listed lines, or that does not parse, is still unknown, and still throws. Current versions are never refused.

A line marked `"current": true` is `Active` on every date and carries no `security_until`: the policy says the line is current, and the reader does not guess when it stops being so.

### Higher[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/support-states.html#higher)

CREED itself requires PHP `^8.3`, like every stack package, and CI tests it on 8.3, 8.4 and 8.5. The policy's floor for apps is a different number: `^8.2` until PHP 8.2 reaches end of life on 2026-12-31, then `^8.3`. Creed has always been one version ahead of everyone else, at least by his own account.

### Related[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/support-states.html#related)

- [Reading the policy from PHP](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/reading-the-policy.html)
- [Reader API](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html)
- [The versions chapter](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/versions.html)

[![CREED's front page: the title page of the Wayne State App Stack Code, 2026 edition, with clause §0.1 spelling out the name, and a green cloth-bound book stamped with CREED's keystone arch mark.](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/readme/hero.jpg)](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/index.html)

## CREED[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/#creed)

![php ^8.3](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/readme/badges/php.svg) ![license MIT](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/readme/badges/license.svg) ![policy schema v1, 6 components](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/readme/badges/policy.svg)

**The standard everything rests on.**

**Not to be confused with:** CREED is the rules; PROCTOR checks an app against them.

This page orients you: what CREED is, what it ships, and where to go next.

CREED is the Wayne State app stack's version policy, as data. One file, `policy/policy.json`, lists the support dates for PHP, Laravel, Node, MySQL, Vue and Inertia, plus the rules every check runs against. A small framework-free PHP reader, `Waynestate\Creed\Policy`, answers the one question every tool needs: what state is this version in, on this date?

### Usage[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/#usage)

```php
use Waynestate\Creed\Policy;
use Waynestate\Creed\State;

$policy = Policy::bundled();

// What state is PHP 8.2 in, on this date?
$state = $policy->stateOf('php', '8.2', new DateTimeImmutable('2026-10-27'));
// State::Security

// What is the oldest PHP an app may declare?
$floor = $policy->oldestSupported('php', new DateTimeImmutable('2026-10-27'));
// '8.2'
```

### Pick your path[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/#pick-your-path)

- [Quick start](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html): the shortest path from `composer require` to a stamped answer.
- [Install](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html): require the package, verify the bundled policy, develop on it.
- [Reader API](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html): every public member of the reader, one line each.
- [Handbook](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/handbook.html): the rules, chapter by chapter.

Status: version 0.1.7, MIT license.

Agents: fetch [https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/llms.txt](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/llms.txt).

One command, two clouds, zero excuses. Higher.

## Install[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html#install)

This page gets you from an empty project to a working CREED reader, and shows how to build and test CREED itself.

### Requirements[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html#requirements)

CREED requires PHP `^8.3`. Its `composer.json` says so, and pins the platform to `8.3.0` so installs resolve against that floor. The reader is framework-free, so nothing else is required at runtime.

### Install[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html#install-1)

Add the package to your project:

```sh
composer require waynestate/creed
```

#### Develop on it[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html#develop-on-it)

The same commands work in PowerShell and sh:

- Windows (PowerShell): `composer install`, then `composer ci` for everything CI runs, or `composer test` for just the tests.
- Linux and macOS (sh): the very same three commands, `composer install`, `composer ci`, `composer test`.

With only Docker (the same line works in PowerShell and sh):

```sh
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app composer:2.10.3 sh -c "composer install --no-interaction && composer ci"
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app php:8.5-cli vendor/bin/phpunit
```

The whole band fits in three commands, and nobody needs a solo.

### Verify[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html#verify)

Load the bundled policy and ask it what state a version is in:

```php
use Waynestate\Creed\Policy;
use Waynestate\Creed\State;

$policy = Policy::bundled();

// What state is PHP 8.2 in, on this date?
$state = $policy->stateOf('php', '8.2', new DateTimeImmutable('2026-10-27'));
// State::Security
```

Expected result: `State::Security`. The reader answers, it does not guess, so if you get a different answer, the date or the policy file is not what you think it is.

### Next steps[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html#next-steps)

Ask the reader two questions in the [Quick start](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html), or read every public member in the [Reader API](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html).

## Reader API[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#reader-api)

This page lists every public member of the `Waynestate\Creed\Policy` reader, in the order the README introduces them, with the signature from `src/Policy.php`.

| Member | What it does | Signature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Policy::bundled()` | Load a policy | `public static function bundled(): self` |
| `Policy::fromFile($path)` | Load a policy | `public static function fromFile(string $path): self` |
| `Policy::fromArray($data)` | Load a policy | `public static function fromArray(array $data): self` |
| `origin()` | Says where it came from | `public function origin(): string` |
| `stateOf($component, $version, $on)` | The state, or an exception | `public function stateOf(string $component, string $version, DateTimeImmutable $on): State` |
| `tryStateOf()` | The same answer as `null` when it cannot be answered | `public function tryStateOf(string $component, ?string $version, DateTimeImmutable $on): ?State` |
| `oldestSupported($component, $on)` | The lowest version still Active or Security | `public function oldestSupported(string $component, DateTimeImmutable $on): ?string` |
| `supported()` | Lists all of them, oldest first | `public function supported(string $component, DateTimeImmutable $on): array` |
| `latestPatch($component, $version)` | The current patch in that line | `public function latestPatch(string $component, string $version): ?string` |
| `latestPatchChecked()` | Says when it was last checked | `public function latestPatchChecked(string $component, string $version): ?string` |
| `line($component, $version)` | The raw line, with `active_until`, `security_until`, `latest_patch`, `latest_patch_checked` (each a string or null) and `current` (true or null) | `public function line(string $component, string $version): ?array` |
| `requires($component, $version)` | The line's `requires` object as an array (`php` range, `mysql` and `mariadb` minimums), or null | `public function requires(string $component, string $version): ?array` |
| `phpRange($component, $version)` | The line's PHP range as `['min' => ..., 'max' => ...]`, or null | `public function phpRange(string $component, string $version): ?array` |
| `activeUntil()` | Those dates as `DateTimeImmutable`, or null | `public function activeUntil(string $component, string $version): ?DateTimeImmutable` |
| `securityUntil()` | Those dates as `DateTimeImmutable`, or null | `public function securityUntil(string $component, string $version): ?DateTimeImmutable` |
| `daysToEol($component, $version, $on)` | Whole days until `security_until`, signed | `public function daysToEol(string $component, string $version, DateTimeImmutable $on): ?int` |
| `isPastGrace()` | Says whether the grace period is over | `public function isPastGrace(string $component, string $version, DateTimeImmutable $on): bool` |
| `resolveVersion($component, $version)` | The policy line a full version like `8.3.12` belongs to | `public function resolveVersion(string $component, string $version): ?string` |
| `isAheadOfPolicy($component, $version)` | Whether a version sorts above every line the policy lists | `public function isAheadOfPolicy(string $component, string $version): bool` |
| `belowOldestLineReason($component, $version)` | The reason a version is `Eol` for sorting below every listed line, or null | `public function belowOldestLineReason(string $component, string $version): ?string` |
| `hasComponent()` | The shape of the policy itself | `public function hasComponent(string $component): bool` |
| `components()` | The shape of the policy itself | `public function components(): array` |
| `versions($component)` | The shape of the policy itself | `public function versions(string $component): array` |
| `tools()` | The shape of the policy itself | `public function tools(): array` |
| `toolMinimum($tool)` | The shape of the policy itself | `public function toolMinimum(string $tool): ?string` |
| `rules()` | The shape of the policy itself | `public function rules(): array` |

Note

The wording is the README's, one line per member; the signatures are copied from `src/Policy.php`.

## Commands and exit codes[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/commands.html#commands-and-exit-codes)

This page lists every command CREED ships, what each one does, and the exit codes the refresh tools return.

### Composer scripts[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/commands.html#composer-scripts)

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `composer install` | Installs the project dependencies. |
| `composer ci` | All checks, what CI runs, in order: `composer validate --strict`, the tests, the policy validator, Pint, the handbook lint, the handbook site and agent-ready freshness checks, PHPStan, `composer audit` and the docs site freshness check. The same command runs on GitLab and GitHub. |
| `composer test` | Only the tests. |
| `composer validate-policy` | Validate `policy.json` against its schema. |
| `composer lint-handbook` | Lint the handbook. |
| `composer fix` | Fix code style. |
| `composer docs` | Rebuild `site/docs/` from `docs/` with the shared docs builder (SQUIRE's kit). |
| `composer docs:check` | Fail when `site/docs/` is stale against `docs/`, a nav path has no page, or a page fails the builder's checks. |
| `composer site:handbook` | Rebuild `site/handbook/` from `handbook/*.md`. |
| `composer site:handbook-check` | Fail when `site/handbook/` is stale against `handbook/*.md`. |
| `composer site:agent-ready` | Rewrite the Markdown twins, `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`, `robots.txt` and `sitemap.xml` in `site/` (SQUIRE's agent-ready kit). |
| `composer site:agent-ready-check` | Fail when those agent-ready files are stale. |
| `composer analyse` | PHPStan. |

Tip

On Windows, if tests fail oddly after a Docker install, delete `vendor/` and install again.

The whole band fits in three commands, and nobody needs a solo.

### The php bin/\*.php tools[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/commands.html#the-php-bin-php-tools)

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `php bin/refresh-patches.php` | Refreshes the `latest_patch` and `latest_patch_checked` fields of the PHP, Laravel, and Node versions in `policy/policy.json` from the upstream feeds, and proposes new Vue lines from endoflife.date. |
| `php bin/refresh-policy.php` | Refreshes `policy/policy.json` from the canonical upstream feeds: support dates, latest patches, and new version lines, with provenance recorded in `policy/sources.json`. |
| `php bin/policy-bot.php run [--dry-run] [--offline <dir>]` | The CREED policy robot: it runs `bin/refresh-policy.php`, reads the run report, commits the policy data on `auto/policy-refresh` as a merge request labeled `auto-data`, and keeps its `auto-alert` issues in line. `--dry-run` prints the plan and changes nothing. See [The policy robot](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-bot.html). |
| `php bin/export.php` | Exports a namespace-prefixed copy of the CREED reader for a consumer package to carry under its own namespace, so two tools in one app never fight over a class name. |
| `php bin/validate-policy.php` | Validates `policy/policy.json` against `policy/policy.schema.json`, and validates `policy/sources.json` against `policy/sources.schema.json` when present. |
| `php bin/lint-handbook.php` | Lints the CREED handbook for RFC 2119 discipline. |
| `php bin/build-handbook-site.php` | Builds the handbook pages of the CREED site from `handbook/*.md`. |
| `php bin/agent-ready.php` | Makes a static front page readable by agents: writes the Markdown twins, `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`, `robots.txt` and `sitemap.xml` into the site folder. |
| `php bin/docs-site.php` | Turns every Markdown file under `docs/` into a committed, accessible, WayneUI-styled docs site under `site/docs/`, and fails CI when the committed pages are stale. |

### Exit codes[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/commands.html#exit-codes)

#### refresh-policy[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/commands.html#refresh-policy)

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | Nothing worth committing was written (and always `0` with `--dry-run`). |
| `1` | A hard failure: unreadable policy, unwritable file, bad option. |
| `3` | Something was written to `policy/policy.json` or `policy/sources.json`: tighten, neutral or loosen-warning changes, a loosen-fail released on proof (still reported as an alert by the policy robot), a first sighting in `policy/sources.json`, or a `--touch` heartbeat. |
| `4` | Something was held or refused. Whatever could be written was written; the held or refused items stay out. The policy robot opens a merge request without auto-merge and an `auto-alert` issue per item. |

The refresher never commits; the policy robot does.

#### policy-bot run[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/commands.html#policy-bot-run)

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | Every handled outcome: nothing to do, a merge request pushed (or nothing staged), the alert issues synced, or a dry run. |
| `1` | The refresher hard-failed or could not start, a required CI variable is missing (named in the output), a git step failed, or the alert issues could not be synced. |

#### refresh-patches[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/commands.html#refresh-patches)

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | Nothing to change (or `--dry-run` with nothing to change). |
| `1` | A feed could not be fetched or parsed. |
| `3` | The policy was updated (or `--dry-run` with changes to show). In CI the scheduled job is check-only: when the policy changed, the tool exits 3 and the job fails on the diff. |

#### export --check[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/commands.html#export-check)

`export --check` compares the copy against a fresh export and exits `1` naming every file that differs, is missing, or is an extra `.php`/`.json` file. In short: it fails when the copy drifts from the source.

### With only Docker[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/commands.html#with-only-docker)

The same lines work in PowerShell and sh.

#### Install and run every check[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/commands.html#install-and-run-every-check)

No PHP on the machine? Fine. Docker runs the suite:

## Configuration[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/configuration.html#configuration)

This page lists the environment CREED reads and the options of `bin/refresh-policy.php`.

### Environment variables[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/configuration.html#environment-variables)

| Variable | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `CREED_BOT_TOKEN` | A CI/CD variable holding the project access token for the policy robot. Masked and hidden, protected, not a file. The schedule runs on `main`, which is a protected branch, so the protected variable is available there. Without the token the `policy-bot` job prints "CREED_BOT_TOKEN not set; skipping the policy robot" and stays green. |
| `CREED_JOB` | A pipeline schedule variable, set to `policy-bot` on the robot's schedule (on `main`, every Monday). The `policy-bot` job in `.gitlab-ci.yml` runs `bin/policy-bot.php run` on that schedule and by hand from the web; the check-only `refresh-patches` job skips it. |

`src/Bot/PolicyBot.php` also reads seven GitLab predefined variables, which every GitLab job has: `CI_API_V4_URL` and `CI_PROJECT_ID` for the alert issues, and `CI_SERVER_PROTOCOL`, `CI_SERVER_HOST`, `CI_SERVER_PORT`, `CI_PROJECT_PATH` and `CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH` for the push. A real run checks the first set before it refreshes and the second before it commits; when one is missing it names it and stops with exit 1, before any push. A `--dry-run` needs none of them.

Warning

The token is masked, hidden and protected, and never printed. Every line the robot prints, including runner errors and command echoes, passes through one mask function that replaces the token value with `[masked]`, so a runner error that echoes the URL back never leaks it.

### refresh-policy options[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/configuration.html#refresh-policy-options)

```
php bin/refresh-policy.php [--dry-run] [--offline <dir>] [--policy <path>]
    [--sources <path>] [--report <file>] [--today YYYY-MM-DD] [--touch]
```

| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--dry-run` | Print what would change without writing anything. |
| `--offline <dir>` | Read the feeds from `<dir>` instead of fetching them. Expects the feed files named after each source in `tests/fixtures/feeds/`. |
| `--policy <path>` | Path to the policy file (default: `policy/policy.json`). |
| `--sources <path>` | Path to the provenance ledger (default: `sources.json` next to the policy). |
| `--report <file>` | Also write a machine-readable report of the run. The report is JSON with `changes`, `held`, `refused`, `disagreements` and `source_errors`. |
| `--today YYYY-MM-DD` | Pretend today is this date (deterministic runs). |
| `--touch` | Set `refreshed_on` to today even when nothing else changed: the robot's weekly heartbeat. |

## Policy file format[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/policy-format.html#policy-file-format)

This page shows the shape of `policy/policy.json` and `policy/sources.json`, exactly as their schemas state it.

CREED is the Wayne State app stack's version policy, as data. One file, `policy/policy.json`, lists the support dates for PHP, Laravel, Node, MySQL, Vue and Inertia, plus the rules every check runs against. The schema titles the file "CREED version policy", requires `schema_version`, `components` and `rules`, and allows no other top-level properties.

### Top level of policy/policy.json[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/policy-format.html#top-level-of-policy-policy-json)

| Name | Type | What the schema states |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schema_version` | integer | Must be exactly `1`. Required. |
| `refreshed_on` | string | A date in `YYYY-MM-DD` form. Optional. |
| `components` | object | At least one entry. Each entry is a component holding a `versions` object, and nothing else. Required. |
| `tools` | object | Maps tool names to a minimum version each. Optional. |
| `rules` | object | The rules every check runs against. Required. |

### The line fields[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/policy-format.html#the-line-fields)

Each component holds a `versions` object that maps a version to a line. Every line may carry these fields:

| Name | Type | What the schema states |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `released` | string | A date. Optional. |
| `active_until` | string | A date. Optional. |
| `security_until` | string | A date. Required on every line except one marked `"current": true`, where it must be absent. |
| `latest_patch` | string | Any string. Optional. |
| `latest_patch_checked` | string | A date. Optional. |
| `current` | boolean | Marks the line as current. Optional. |
| `requires` | object | May hold `php` (an object with required `min` and `max`, each a version string matching `^\d+(\.\d+)*$`) and `mysql` and `mariadb` (each a version string matching the same pattern), and nothing else. Optional. The bundled policy fills it for the Laravel lines, from Laravel's release notes and database pages. |
| `images` | object | May hold `citadel`, `docker`, `openshift` and `coolify`, each a non-empty string. Optional. Today `docker` is filled for PHP 8.3 to 8.5; the other keys are not filled. |

The `current` rule is the only conditional in the schema: a line with `"current": true` must not carry `security_until`, and every other line must.

### tools[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/policy-format.html#tools)

`tools` is optional. Its property names must match `^[a-z][a-z0-9-]*$`, and each value is an object with one required field:

| Name | Type | What the schema states |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `minimum` | string | Matches `^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$`, a major.minor.patch version. Required inside each tool. |

### rules[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/policy-format.html#rules)

`rules` allows exactly three properties, all required:

| Name | Type | What the schema states |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `audit_severity_threshold` | string | Required. |
| `banned_constraints` | array of strings | Required. |
| `eol_grace_days` | integer | Minimum `0`. Required. |

### policy/sources.json[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/policy-format.html#policy-sources-json)

The schema titles `policy/sources.json` the "CREED refresh provenance ledger". It records, per observed value, which source said it and the first and last day it was seen.

| Name | Type | What the schema states |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schema_version` | integer | Must be exactly `1`. Required. |
| `updated_on` | string | A date in `YYYY-MM-DD` form. Optional. |
| `observations` | object | Nested objects, down to one record per observed value. Required. |

Each leaf record carries exactly three fields:

| Name | Type | What the schema states |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `value` | string | Required. |
| `first_seen` | string | A date in `YYYY-MM-DD` form. Required. |
| `last_seen` | string | A date in `YYYY-MM-DD` form. Required. |

### Schema version and older readers[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/policy-format.html#schema-version-and-older-readers)

The schema is `version: 1`. Optional new fields keep it at 1; a breaking schema change needs a new version and a release of every reader. The schema is strict: unknown keys fail CREED's own CI. Readers are tolerant: unknown keys are ignored, so older readers keep working on a newer file. The older-reader contract is pinned by `tests/OlderReaderContractTest.php`; change the fixture only with a `schema_version` bump.

### A real excerpt[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/policy-format.html#a-real-excerpt)

One real line from `policy/policy.json`, verbatim (the PHP 8.2 entry):

```json
"8.2": {
    "active_until": "2024-12-31",
    "security_until": "2026-12-31",
    "latest_patch": "8.2.35",
    "latest_patch_checked": "2026-10-28"
},
```

Note

Creed Bratton's past is a mystery. Ours is in `policy/policy.json`, where it belongs.

## Proof[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/proof.html#proof)

This page shows where CREED proves itself against real Wayne State applications and what the `composer ci` gate checks before anything ships.

### Where the proof runs[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/proof.html#where-the-proof-runs)

Proof runs against real Wayne State applications are on a private site, [proof.apps.wayne.edu/creed](https://proof.apps.wayne.edu/creed/), behind a Wayne State employee sign-in.

Note

The front page, [`site/index.html`](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/), is a static page you can open in a browser or serve from `site/`. On Citadel it is served by the raw-PHP deploy layer in `deploy/`: a Squire kit whose front controller serves `site/` behind HELMET's security headers. For local development, keep serving `site/` directly.

### What `composer ci` proves[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/proof.html#what-composer-ci-proves)

`composer ci` is the same command on GitLab and GitHub. It validates `composer.json`, runs the test suite (280 tests in 23 files on 2026-11-06), validates `policy/policy.json` and `policy/sources.json` against their schemas, checks style with Pint, lints the handbook, runs PHPStan and `composer audit`, and fails when the handbook site, the agent-ready files or the docs pages go stale, so the site you are reading cannot drift from `docs/`.

Where it runs: GitHub runs `composer ci` on PHP 8.3, 8.4 and 8.5. GitLab runs the test suite on all three through Preflight's `php-test` component, and `composer ci` once on the pinned Composer image (PHP 8.5). GitLab also runs PROCTOR against the front page's `deploy/` layer (allowed to fail while its known findings stand) and the strict WayneUI copies check.

The policy itself is proved every Monday: the [policy robot](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-bot.html) re-reads the upstream sources and opens a merge request when anything moved.

### The badges[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/proof.html#the-badges)

The README carries four badges:

- `php ^8.3`: CREED itself requires PHP `^8.3`, like every stack package.
- `license MIT`.
- `policy schema v1, 6 components`: the schema is `version: 1`, and the policy lists the support dates for PHP, Laravel, Node, MySQL, Vue and Inertia.
- GitHub CI: the status of the `composer ci` workflow on the mirror.

Creed Bratton keeps his records in a filing cabinet nobody can find; ours are in `docs/`, where anyone can.

## Troubleshooting[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/troubleshooting.html#troubleshooting)

Answers to the failures that look alarming but are expected, each with the page that explains the behavior.

### Why did the scheduled `refresh-patches` job fail?[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/troubleshooting.html#why-did-the-scheduled-refresh-patches-job-fail)

A scheduled `refresh-patches` failure is expected whenever upstream ships a patch. The scheduled job is check-only: when the policy changed, the tool exits 3 and the job fails on the diff. Treat the red run as a to-do, not an outage. On GitLab the policy robot's Monday merge request usually carries the same patch already: review and merge that one. Otherwise run `php bin/refresh-patches.php`, read the diff, run `composer ci`, add a CHANGELOG line, and commit. The [Changelog](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/changelog.html) is where that line goes.

### Why does the `policy-bot` job print "CREED_BOT_TOKEN not set; skipping the policy robot" and stay green?[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/troubleshooting.html#why-does-the-policy-bot-job-print-creed-bot-token-not-set-skipping-the-policy-robot-and-stay-green)

That is the designed behavior when the masked `CREED_BOT_TOKEN` CI variable is not set: the job prints the line and stays green. Missing CI variables stop the run before any push, so nothing is committed. The job runs on its dedicated schedule (the one carrying `CREED_JOB=policy-bot`) and by hand from the web. It landed in 0.1.6; see the [Changelog](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/changelog.html).

### Why can the robot not push when `auto/policy-refresh` is protected?[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/troubleshooting.html#why-can-the-robot-not-push-when-auto-policy-refresh-is-protected)

The branch `auto/policy-refresh` must not be protected, or the robot cannot push it. The robot commits `policy/policy.json` and `policy/sources.json` on that branch and force-pushes it as a merge request labeled `auto-data`. Branch protection is a project setting, not a file in this repo; [The policy robot](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-bot.html) has the whole setup.

### Why did the robot's merge request not merge itself?[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/troubleshooting.html#why-did-the-robot-s-merge-request-not-merge-itself)

Two reasons, both on purpose. A run whose refresher exited 4 (something held or refused) opens its merge request without auto-merge, so a person decides; the held or refused items are listed in the body and each has an `auto-alert` issue. And an exit 3 merge request merges only when its pipeline passes, so a red `composer ci` holds it, even when the failure has nothing to do with the policy (a fresh security advisory in `composer audit`, say). Fix the failure on `main`, then rebase the merge request or start the robot by hand on `main`; re-running the old pipeline tests the old branch again. Never commit to `auto/policy-refresh`: the next Monday overwrites it. [Reviewing what it opens](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy-bot.html#reviewing-what-it-opens) walks through it.

### Tests fail oddly on Windows after a Docker install[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/troubleshooting.html#tests-fail-oddly-on-windows-after-a-docker-install)

Delete `vendor/` and install again. The install and Docker paths are in [Install](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html).

### `composer ci` fails because the docs site or handbook site is stale[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/troubleshooting.html#composer-ci-fails-because-the-docs-site-or-handbook-site-is-stale)

Rebuild the stale side: `composer docs` rebuilds the docs site from `docs/`, and `composer site:handbook` rebuilds the handbook site. [Proof](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/proof.html) covers what `composer ci` checks, including the stale-page failure.

### What is the difference between `refresh-policy` exit 3 and exit 4?[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/troubleshooting.html#what-is-the-difference-between-refresh-policy-exit-3-and-exit-4)

Exit 3 means something was written to `policy/policy.json` or `policy/sources.json`, including a released `loosen-fail` (the policy robot raises the alert from the report). Exit 4 means something was held or refused: whatever could be written was written, the held or refused items stayed out, and the policy robot opens its merge request without auto-merge. The refresher itself never commits. Exit 0 means nothing worth committing, and exit 1 is a hard failure. Version 0.1.2 changed a released loosening from exit 4 to exit 3; see the [Changelog](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/changelog.html).

### Why does the reader throw for a version between listed lines, or one that does not parse?[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/troubleshooting.html#why-does-the-reader-throw-for-a-version-between-listed-lines-or-one-that-does-not-parse)

The reader refuses what it does not know, except the newest thing and the oldest. A version that sorts above every line the policy lists is `Active`, and a version that parses and sorts below every listed line is `Eol`, with the reason from `belowOldestLineReason()`. A version that falls between listed lines, or that does not parse, is still unknown, and still throws. Unlisted components are refused the same way. Current versions are never refused. The handbook's [Dependencies](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/dependencies.html) chapter explains the states.

Creed Bratton would not care, but he is not reviewing the merge request.

## Upgrading[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/upgrading.html#upgrading)

How CREED versions are cut, what each release changed that a consumer notices, and which consumers must refresh a generated copy after a policy change.

### How versions are cut[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/upgrading.html#how-versions-are-cut)

1. Move the lines under `## Unreleased` in `CHANGELOG.md` to a new `## X.Y.Z (YYYY-MM-DD)` heading, leaving an empty `## Unreleased`. (0.1.0 predates the heading convention, so it has none.)
2. `composer ci` green locally, then on both pipelines for that commit.
3. Run a secrets scan of the history and check that nothing internal (server names, people, IDs) is in the tree.
4. Tag `X.Y.Z` (no `v`) on git.wayne.edu. The mirror carries the tag to GitHub, and Packagist picks it up from there.
5. A release needs a maintainer's approval. Never move or delete a published tag.
6. Then bump `waynestate/creed` where the stack pins it, and refresh the generated copies.

### 0.1.7 (2026-11-07)[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/upgrading.html#0-1-7-2026-11-07)

The policy records, per Laravel line, the PHP versions it supports and the minimum MySQL and MariaDB versions, in a new optional `requires` field on the line. A policy file that uses `requires` fails validation against the 0.1.6 schema, so a publisher updates the schema first. Readers ignore the field, so an older reader keeps working on a newer file. The same holds for the new optional `images` object on a line (`images.docker` is filled for PHP 8.3 to 8.5).

Nothing changes for a consumer in how the policy is kept: the policy robot's Monday merge requests land in `policy/policy.json` like any other commit, so a consumer that carries a copy refreshes it after a release as before.

### 0.1.6 (2026-11-03)[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/upgrading.html#0-1-6-2026-11-03)

A `policy-bot` CI job runs `bin/policy-bot.php run` with `CREED_BOT_TOKEN` on a weekly schedule (the one carrying `CREED_JOB=policy-bot`) or by hand; without the token it skips green, and the check-only `refresh-patches` job now skips that schedule. Docs and package metadata name nougat as the canonical repository, with git.wayne.edu and GitHub as read-only mirrors, until git.wayne.edu has CI runners.

### 0.1.5 (2026-11-03)[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/upgrading.html#0-1-5-2026-11-03)

The handbook grew: new chapters Secrets and Production from the WSU developer standards (2024), WSU developer standards (2024) rules in the Code, Auth, Databases, Dependencies and CI chapters, a note on MySQL lines and auth plugin, and BEST_PRACTICES section 11 (practices 55 to 61). Handbook rules now name the PROCTOR check that enforces them. The BEST_PRACTICES statements and gap list were fixed to match the tree, schema and tests. A test pins that an older reader accepts a newer policy file. CI pulls its Docker Hub images through the GitLab Dependency Proxy, a `wayneui-copies` gate job was added, and the unused `composer/semver` dependency was removed.

### 0.1.4 (2026-10-30)[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/upgrading.html#0-1-4-2026-10-30)

The bot's GitLab HTTP client failed on every API call (`stream_context_create` options were not under the `http` wrapper, a ValueError on current PHP). It now works and reads response headers from the stream's metadata, so PHP 8.5 shows no deprecation. The deploy layer's Squire kit was refreshed to 0.3.3 and then 0.3.4 (the local `.env.squire` file is now git-ignored).

### 0.1.3 (2026-10-29)[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/upgrading.html#0-1-3-2026-10-29)

The proof page moved to a private site that needs a Wayne State sign-in. Project names are written as words except acronyms. A real `bin/policy-bot.php run` now commits the data allowlist on `auto/policy-refresh` and force-pushes it with GitLab merge request push options (create, target, remove source branch, label `auto-data`, title; `merge_request.auto_merge` on exit 3 only); missing variables stop the run with exit 1 naming them, and every printed line masks the token as `[masked]`. After an exit 0, a refresh whose `refreshed_on` is 7 or more days old runs the refresher again with `--touch`. The robot keeps its GitLab alert issues in line with the report, one open issue per alert key, each labelled `auto-alert`. New `src/Bot/GitLabClient.php` is a small GitLab API client over an injectable `HttpTransport`, shipped with a dependency-free PHP streams transport; the token rides only in the `PRIVATE-TOKEN` header, never in a URL. Stale capability claims in the site and docs were fixed.

### 0.1.2 (2026-10-29)[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/upgrading.html#0-1-2-2026-10-29)

`bin/refresh-policy.php`: a released version that loosens a constraint now exits 3 (changes written) with an alert in the report, instead of exit 4. Reader behavior: a version of a known component that is older than the oldest listed line (PHP 5.x to 8.0, Laravel 5 to 8, Inertia 0.x) is now `Eol`, with the reason `older than the oldest listed line (8.1)` from the new `belowOldestLineReason($component, $version)`, instead of being refused as an unknown version. Unlisted components and version strings that do not parse are still refused, and a version above every listed line is still `Active`.

### 0.1.1 (2026-10-29)[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/upgrading.html#0-1-1-2026-10-29)

`bin/refresh-policy.php` keeps every support date, patch and new line tied to a canonical source (php.net, the Node.js release schedule, endoflife.date, Packagist, npm). Changes are classed tighten, neutral, loosen-warning or loosen-fail; a later security date is held until two sources agree or 14 days pass; nothing is ever removed. Provenance lives in the new `policy/sources.json` (schema and validation included), and the policy gains an optional `refreshed_on` date. Policy lines may be marked `"current": true`: Active on every date, with no `security_until`; the schema rejects a current line that also carries a `security_until`, and a line that carries neither. `stateOf()` resolves a version to its policy line before judging it: a version that sorts above every listed line is `Active` (current versions are never refused), while a version between listed lines still throws. New reader method `isAheadOfPolicy($component, $version)`; `line()` reports a fifth field, `current` (true or null). The bundled policy lists Vue 3 and Inertia 2 as current lines. `bin/refresh-patches.php` reads the endoflife.date Vue feed and proposes new Vue lines alongside the patch refresh. The README's reader example is now a test: `tests/ReadmeTest.php` runs every PHP code block that uses the reader against the bundled policy and asserts the values printed beside it. The handbook is now linted for RFC 2119 capitalization, every chapter declares RFC 2119 and uses capital keywords, and `handbook/databases.md` gains a "Grace period" section spelling out the 90-day `eol_grace_days` window (`Security` on `security_until`, `Eol` for the window, `EolGraceExpired` after, no override). `handbook/dependencies.md` gains a "Private packages" section. PHPStan now includes Pinstripe's raw preset instead of carrying a hand copy.

### 0.1.0 (2026-10-27)[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/upgrading.html#0-1-0-2026-10-27)

First tagged release.

### Which consumers must refresh a generated copy[#](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/docs/upgrading.html#which-consumers-must-refresh-a-generated-copy)

PROCTOR, Rollcall and Booster each carry a generated copy of the reader under their own namespace, so two tools in one app never fight over a class name; ADVISOR carries CREED's policy and handbook as a data bundle instead. After any policy change, the copies downstream are stale until refreshed. In each consumer (PROCTOR, Rollcall, Booster), run `php <creed>/bin/export.php --namespace='Waynestate\<Project>\Creed' --to=src/Creed`, then `composer creed-copy:check` with `CREED_PATH` pointing at this checkout. ADVISOR regenerates with `content:generate`.

Creed Bratton would have a form for this.

Chapter 9

## Accessibility

4 sections · 9 provisions · **MUST NOT** 1 · **SHOULD** 1

Decided

Key words The key words **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **SHOULD**, **SHOULD NOT** and **MAY** in this chapter are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119).

### [§9.1](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/accessibility.html#target) Target

- Every public page of a stack app targets WCAG 2.2 Level AA (the stack's accessibility design).
- W3C says content conforming to 2.2 also conforms to 2.1 and 2.0, so the target meets the WCAG 2.1 AA floor named in the ADA Title II web rule (the stack's accessibility design).

### [§9.2](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/accessibility.html#components) Components

- [WayneUI](https://wayneui.apps.wayne.edu/) is the stack's component library; pages built from its components start from markup and tokens already checked by WayneUI's own runnable accessibility gate (the stack's accessibility design).
- An app **MUST NOT** fork or restyle a WayneUI component in a way that removes focus indicators, labels or contrast (the stack's accessibility design). [PROCTOR](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/) check: `wayneui-forked-views` catches forked views.

### [§9.3](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/accessibility.html#checks) Checks

- An automated accessibility check **SHOULD** run in CI on the app's key pages. GitLab's accessibility testing uses Pa11y and is available on every self-managed tier (the stack's accessibility design).
- An automated tool catches regressions; it is not proof of conformance, and it never replaces a manual keyboard and screen reader pass before launch (the stack's accessibility design).
- [Preflight](https://preflight.apps.wayne.edu/) has no accessibility component yet (not built yet).

### [§9.4](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/accessibility.html#not-decided-here) Not decided here

- Whether and when the ADA Title II web rule applies to a given WSU unit. The rule applies WCAG 2.1 AA to public entities on dates that depend on the entity's size; the answer is for WSU's counsel and accessibility office, and this chapter does not decide it.
- Which pages need a manual audit.

Set from [`handbook/accessibility.md` on GitHub](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/handbook/accessibility.md), impression `977069b`. Found a mistake? Fix the Markdown; this page is rebuilt from it.

Chapter 4

## Auth

12 provisions · **MUST** 3

Partly decided

Key words The key words **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **SHOULD**, **SHOULD NOT** and **MAY** in this chapter are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119).

- One protocol-neutral library, named for what it does, not how. It returns a verified identity and leaves the session to the app (the stack's auth design).
- The app always owns its session. Every driver ends in the app's `findOrImportUser(identity)`, and the protocol never holds the session (the stack's auth design).
- The `gateway` driver accepts only a signed assertion, never a bare header: user, attributes, issued-at, audience, an expiry of 60 seconds or less, and a signature the gateway and app share (the stack's auth design).
- Drivers: `cas` (the default today), `gateway`, `oidc`, `oauth2`, `saml` (not built yet), and `fake` for local development and tests (the stack's auth design).
- Non-EOL PHP only, with no exceptions (the stack's auth design). [PROCTOR](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/) check: `php-floor`.
- To be decided: the gateway's key distribution and rotation, and the SAML library choice if a `saml` driver is built (the stack's auth design).
- API and other stateless requests are authenticated with signed, short-lived bearer tokens in an `Authorization` header, verified on every request. A token is signed, not merely encrypted; JSON Web Tokens are a good fit (WSU developer standards, 2024).
- Authentication is checked before any content is shown or any script function runs, on every request. Deny by default: routes are protected unless listed as public, and an unauthenticated person is sent to sign in (WSU developer standards, 2024).
- When authentication or an authorization lookup fails, the result is fail closed: access is withheld (WSU developer standards, 2024).
- Administrative access **MUST** be limited to named users or roles, and access that is due to end is revoked on a regular schedule (WSU developer standards, 2024).
- Access that is due to end when a person's status changes (for example an ended employment) **MUST** be removed by an automated process, not by memory (WSU developer standards, 2024).
- Idle sessions **MUST** time out after a configurable period of inactivity. The stack sets no number yet; Laravel's default session lifetime applies until it does (WSU developer standards, 2024).

Set from [`handbook/auth.md` on GitHub](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/handbook/auth.md), impression `5b8bf9e`. Found a mistake? Fix the Markdown; this page is rebuilt from it.

Source: https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/ci.html

Chapter 8

## CI

8 provisions · **MUST** 2 · **SHOULD** 1

Decided

Key words The key words **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **SHOULD**, **SHOULD NOT** and **MAY** in this chapter are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119).

- CI is enforcement point (c): a red pipeline before merge (the stack's enforcement design). [PROCTOR](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/) check: `ci-pipelines`.
- The CI components are [Preflight](https://preflight.apps.wayne.edu/)'s: `proctor`, `php-test` and `composer-audit`, included with `include: component:` (first-repos).
- CI judges with deterministic commands, never with a model. No gate depends on a model's opinion (the stack's rule on language models).
- Components are pinned at a tag or SHA, never `~latest` (first-repos).
- The components run on the git.wayne.edu instance runner (first-repos), and every product strongly recommends the instance runner.
- Every change lands through a merge request that another person reviews, and critical findings are addressed before merge (**SHOULD** for a one-person project: record the self-review in the merge request) (WSU developer standards, 2024).
- Every project **MUST** have a defined, well-understood change-control process with change requests; review and approval of merge requests is change control only for simple projects, and the process **MUST** be followed strictly (WSU developer standards, 2024).
- Known problem: the change-request procedure on Citadel is currently broken and needs fixing there; until it is fixed, record changes through reviewed merge requests and tell the Citadel team.

Set from [`handbook/ci.md` on GitHub](https://github.com/waynestate/creed/blob/main/handbook/ci.md), impression `8802e0e`. Found a mistake? Fix the Markdown; this page is rebuilt from it.

Source: https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html

Chapter 3

## Code

13 sections · 43 provisions · **MUST NOT** 3 · **MUST** 6 · **SHOULD** 2

Partly decided

Key words The key words **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **SHOULD**, **SHOULD NOT** and **MAY** in this chapter are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119).

### [§3.1](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#php-style) PHP style

- Laravel apps use Pint's `laravel` preset (the stack's coding standard).
- Raw PHP apps and the stack's own packages use the `per` preset, PER Coding Style 3.1 (the stack's coding standard).
- One formatter per repo, never two (the stack's coding standard).
- An app points Pint at the preset in `vendor/waynestate/pinstripe/pint/` with `--config` (the stack's coding standard).
- Files are UTF-8 without a BOM, with LF line endings (the stack's every-OS design).

### [§3.2](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#reading-the-code) Reading the code

- Comment where it helps: complex logic, areas that could improve, business rules that would otherwise be a mystery (**SHOULD**). Do not keep version history in comments; git is the change log (WSU developer standards, 2024). No check exists yet.
- Code that no longer runs **MUST** be removed, not commented out; git keeps it (WSU developer standards, 2024). No check exists yet.
- Variable, class and database names **SHOULD** be complete and descriptive; avoid ambiguous abbreviations (WSU developer standards, 2024). No check exists yet.

### [§3.3](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#source-control-and-documentation) Source control and documentation

- All source is kept in git. Access to a repo **MUST** be removed when someone leaves the project or the university (WSU developer standards, 2024). No check exists yet.
- The stack's code has its primary home on git.wayne.edu; the standards name git.wayne.edu as the preferred home.
- Register the project in the catalog Enterprise Apps names, and keep its environments current. Stack apps also register with [Rollcall](https://rollcall.apps.wayne.edu/), the stack's census (WSU developer standards, 2024).
- Every repo's README **MUST** say how to install, configure and deploy the code for local development, on every OS (see `every-os.md`), and how to update an existing deployment (WSU developer standards, 2024). No check exists yet.
- If the Help Desk might be contacted about the project, keep an overview in the repo: what it does, who uses it, known common issues and who to call for an incident; deliver changes to the Help Desk when it changes (WSU developer standards, 2024).

### [§3.4](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#static-analysis) Static analysis

- PHPStan level 8 for new code: the stack's own packages and every app [Sourdough](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/) generates (the stack's coding standard).
- Larastan loads only where Laravel is present (the stack's coding standard).
- Every inline ignore carries an identifier and a reason; configs set `reportIgnoresWithoutComments` (the stack's coding standard).
- PHPStan's `phpVersion` follows the policy's PHP floor (the stack's coding standard).
- Existing apps start at the highest level they pass, with a committed baseline that **MUST NOT** grow, then raise the level one step at a time (the stack's coding standard). No check exists yet. Like the band says, the only way is Higher.
- New packages have no baseline (the stack's coding standard).
- Two reasons for level 8:
  - The starters begin clean, so new apps pass from day one (the stack's coding standard).
  - Null handling is the class of bug level 8 adds; in the stack's auth and header code, a null bug is a security bug (the stack's coding standard).

### [§3.5](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#input-and-files) Input and files

- All input (forms, API calls, headers, cookies, and data read from a database you do not control) **MUST** be validated on the server; SQL uses bound parameters, and output is escaped for where it lands. That guards against SQL injection and cross-site scripting (WSU developer standards, 2024). No check exists yet.
- Files from untrusted sources **MUST** be checked against the expected type, **MUST NOT** be passed to include, class-loading or reflection calls, **MUST** be stored outside the served folder with limited permissions, and **MUST NOT** be executable (WSU developer standards, 2024). No check exists yet.

### [§3.6](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#banned-patterns) Banned patterns

Each ban becomes a PHPStan rule: Larastan's where it has one, `phpstan-disallowed-calls` for plain bans, and a custom rule only when neither fits.

- `env()` only in `config/` files, from Larastan's `NoEnvCallsOutsideOfConfig` rule. [PROCTOR](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/) check: `env-outside-config` (a warning per call); the PHPStan rule is planned.
- No disabled TLS verification, such as `withoutVerifying()` or `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER` set to false (OWASP ASVS). Planned.
- No SQL built by joining strings; use bindings (OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet). Planned.
- No debug leftovers or dynamic code, from `phpstan-disallowed-calls`. Planned.

### [§3.7](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#vue-and-javascript) Vue and JavaScript

- ESLint flat config (the stack's coding standard).
- `eslint-plugin-vue` `flat/recommended` (the stack's coding standard).
- Prettier for formatting (the stack's coding standard).
- `eslint-plugin-vuejs-accessibility` (the stack's coding standard).
- Both JavaScript and TypeScript are linted (the stack's coding standard).
- The stack's Vue starters use TypeScript; plain JavaScript stays fully supported (the stack's coding standard).
- Node 22.13 or newer for the lint tools (the stack's coding standard).

### [§3.8](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#security-analysis) Security analysis

- The stack's GitLab instances run the Free tier, so nothing relies on GitLab SAST (the stack's coding standard).
- The open tools instead: Larastan's env rule, `phpstan-disallowed-calls`, and a Psalm taint-analysis pilot on one app (the stack's coding standard).

### [§3.9](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#how-it-is-enforced) How it is enforced

- Pint, PHPStan, Rector dry-runs and ESLint run in CI through [Preflight](https://preflight.apps.wayne.edu/) components, not in the deploy gate (the stack's coding standard). The Preflight components are Planned.
- New rules arrive as warnings and become errors on a stated date, the same staging as PHP versions (the stack's enforcement design).
- PROCTOR reports whether an app uses the presets (the stack's coding standard). The PROCTOR report is Planned.

### [§3.10](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#which-preset-enforces-each-rule) Which preset enforces each rule

Table 3-1

| Rule | Preset file | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PHP style, Laravel apps | `pint/laravel.json` | Planned |

| Static analysis, raw apps | `phpstan/raw.neon` | Planned |

| Security analysis | to be decided | Planned |

### [§3.11](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#not-adopted) Not adopted

- Mago and PHP_CodeSniffer 4 are not adopted; Pint is the only formatter (the stack's coding standard).
- Mago is looked at again before Pinstripe 1.0 (the stack's coding standard).

### [§3.12](https://creed.apps.wayne.edu/handbook/code.html#to-be-decided) To be decided

- `declare(strict_types=1)` in every file. The sources recommend it, but the stack's coding standard does not decide it.
- `phpstan-strict-rules` for the stack's packages (the stack's coding standard).
- Where the ESLint package is published (the stack's coding standard).
